title: Visual Similarity in Adult Word Extension and Artificial Word Learning
description: arXiv:2611.14116v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When two objects share a name, how much does their visual similarity explain, and what do the teaching examples add? First, we reanalyzed trial-level data from a large adult word-extension study (Lewis & Frank, 2018), computing each test image's distance to the examples shown in the space of a frozen self-supervised visual encoder (DINOv2). Distance was associated with extension (log odds -3.23 per standard deviation; 520 people), and an exploratory post hoc analysis suggested that this association persisted within the taught domain after controlling for taxonomic level and teaching condition. Example composition also mattered: after three examples, adults extended a word to 1.1% of superordinate items when the examples were subordinate and to 77.5% when they were superordinate. Second, in an artificial learner using the same encoder, words joining two categories were learned less accurately the farther apart the categories were (84.7%, 65.4%, and 53.0% naming accuracy for near, mid, and far pairs). The encoder's distances correlated with human similarity and confusability measures from three datasets (rho = .501-.795), but this representational alignment did not translate into conclusive evidence that human-derived distances predict learner difficulty, and a second encoder trained on one child's experience reproduced the tier ordering but not the pair-level effect. The secondary human data were analyzed under an internal plan fixed before the confirmatory analyses (not externally preregistered). Visual similarity accounts for part of how generalization is organized in both systems, while the composition of examples contributes what the distance we used does not capture.

title: CLADE: Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
description: arXiv:2611.14355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented systems often retrieve passages that are accurate and relevant but state the answer at a coarser level of granularity than the question requires. For example, a question may ask which specific disease a drug treats (familial hyperlipidemia), while the retrieved passage mentions the broader disease family (hyperlipidemia). Prior work on context sufficiency treats such coarse passages simply as insufficient. We argue that they form a distinct case, which we call resolvable insufficiency: text alone cannot settle the fine-grained answer, but the broader category it mentions maps to a short list of candidate answers in a domain ontology. When language models read these coarse, family-only passages, they exhibit a phenomenon we call Clade (Category-Level Answering from Deficient Evidence): they answer instead of abstaining or searching further. On biomedical questions from PrimeKG, family-only passages reduce abstention by 13.8 points compared to uninformative passages, and the resulting guesses are wrong about half the time. description: arXiv:2611.14113v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding the progress of an activity requires tracking how the objects involved change over time. title: Are Spiking Neural Networks Harder to Steal? The Role of Stochastic Encoding in Model Extraction
description: arXiv:2610.36298v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning models deployed on edge devices are vulnerable to model stealing attacks, in which an adversary replicates a model using only its predictions. Existing defenses add mechanisms that are costly on resource-constrained hardware. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer energy-efficient inference at the edge and have been shown to leak less information about their training data than artificial neural networks (ANNs). This work investigates whether SNNs also resist model stealing and identifies the source of any such resistance. We evaluate four model stealing attacks against SNN and ANN models on three image datasets and introduce a metric that accounts for the stochastic outputs of SNNs. SNNs therefore protect against model stealing without additional defense mechanisms, but this protection does not withstand adaptive adversaries.

description: arXiv:2502.18733v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep learning's growing prevalence has driven its widespread use in healthcare, where AI and sensor advancements enhance diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring. title: Quantifying the Sampling Frequency Invariance of Time-Series Foundation Models for Sensor Data Applications
description: arXiv:2611.14425v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) are increasingly used in sensor applications, where sampling frequency (SF) varies across sensors, devices, and operating modes (e.g., power saving). In this paper, we stress-test 4 prominent TSFMs: MOMENT, Chronos-2, Moirai-MoE, and TimesFM, to quantify their SF-invariance and investigate whether their behavior tracks the resulting loss of information bandwidth rather than the SF value itself. Our stress-test probes 3 dimensions: (i) the shift in embeddings, (ii) the degradation in forecasting performance, and (iii) the degradation in downstream performance, quantified by three novel metrics: FSI, FDI, and CDI, respectively. To our knowledge, this is the first study to place SF-invariance at the core of TSFM evaluations. Our results characterize: (i) how SF-invariance depends on the margin between signal's native-SF and the bandwidth its task requires, (ii) how much of that invariance the choice of TSFM explains, and (iii) how much of TSFM's performance degradation under a lower SF reflects information loss rather than a limitation of their abilities. These findings reframe SF-invariance as a measurable, signal-aware property of the (signal X TSFM) pair, and guide practitioners on when TSFMs display SF-invariance.

description: arXiv:2611.14111v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous systems increasingly monitor physical kinematics, environmental states and task completion outcomes. In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies. Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations. In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key. Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.

title: STABLE: A Continual Learning Optimizer with Adaptive Drift Control
description: arXiv:2611.10655v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Continual learning suffers from catastrophic forgetting, leading to the loss of past knowledge and unstable adaptation across task streams. Existing approaches typically address this issue through replay buffers, architectural changes, or additional regularization terms. We argue that forgetting is a consequence of unstable learning dynamics, which may benefit from an optimizer-level solution. The main challenge is that learning dynamics are time-dependent, as demonstrated by empirical phenomena such as the stability gap. First, we formally prove that, for distance-based classifiers, bounded parameter drift guarantees bounded margin erosion under a local score-stability condition. Based on this insight, we propose STABLE, a primal-dual optimizer with adaptive drift control. STABLE enforces a drift budget by increasing the dual variable when the budget is violated and decreasing it otherwise. This results in high stability without penalizing plasticity. Experiments on long-horizon unimodal streams and CLIP-based multimodal streams show that vanilla PEFT baselines trained with STABLE match or outperform specialized continual learning methods. In the multimodal setting, STABLE further preserves zero-shot transfer, matching or exceeding dedicated multimodal continual learning methods. Code is available at https://github.com/atlas-luiss/STABLE.

title: You Don't Need Feature Learning to Do In-Context Learning
description: arXiv:2611.13431v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How should we understand memorization vs. generalization in in-context learning (ICL) tasks, and when does one happen vs. the other? To investigate, we study how rotation-invariant kernel machines learn the ICL linear regression task proposed by Raventos et al. (2023). By decomposing the task in the kernel eigenbasis, we obtain a spectral picture of learning in this ICL setting. This picture reveals that as sample size grows, kernel machines learn successively-higher-degree components of the memorizing solution, which depend upon successively-higher-degree statistics of the training task set. The generalizing solution is approximately a low-degree truncation of the memorizing solution, and so the model first generalizes, then degrades into memorization as training proceeds. The takeaways are threefold. First, if this case is indicative, learning a "generalizing" solution on an ICL task is really just underfitting the memorizing solution! Second, the fact that kernel machines can generalize on this task means that feature learning is inessential to ICL. Third, transformers empirically trained to do ICL are shown to memorize tasks through the higher-order statistics of the training tasks that the kernel-based theory predicts, suggesting it applies even to models capable of feature learning.

title: Bits or permutations? Spending a fixed inference budget on weight precision or on option-order averaging in small local language models
description: arXiv:2611.14413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local language models can save memory by storing weights in fewer bits, and they can reduce sensitivity to the order of answer options by averaging a few reorderings. We ask whether the first makes the second worse, and which is the cheaper way to spend a fixed budget. On Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B with simulated round-to-nearest weight quantization (8, 6, 4 and 3 bits, fp16 reference), read from the logits of the letters A to D on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MMLU and HellaSwag (300 items each), 6 bits lose no accuracy against fp16 (they score +1.8 (+1.0 to +2.5) and +0.9 (+0.3 to +1.5) points higher, which we do not explain), and 8 bits change it by -0.7 (-1.1 to -0.3) and -0.4 (-0.7 to -0.2) points. At 4 bits the answer-slot skew rises from 0.15 to 0.53 (0.6B) and from 0.07 to 0.12 (1.7B); Gaussian noise at the same weight SNR gives 0.15 and 0.37 (two draws) and 0.19 (one draw), so the control is inconclusive on whether rounding adds slot skew beyond equal-power noise. Flip rates rise but stay below an accuracy-matched baseline of independent uniform errors. Averaging four cyclic orders recovers +12.6 points at 4 bits for 0.6B (+5.3 at fp16). We price bits and passes in one machine-independent unit, weight bytes read times passes. In cost-matched pairs, extra orders beat extra bits only when the weights have 6 or more bits, and the decision table reduces to: use 6-bit weights and spend the rest of the budget on up to four orders, one pass each. Everything is simulated on two small models with the simplest quantizer; a title-level search found no earlier study of quantization together with option order.

fingerprint: using wearables to enable cardiovascular kidney metabolic ckm risk profiling for personalized coaching|research.google/blog/using-wearables-to-enable-cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic-ckm-risk-profiling
title: Using wearables to enable cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) risk profiling for personalized coaching
description: Health & Bioscience
content: Using wearables to enable cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) risk profiling for personalized coaching November 11, 2026 Zeinab Esmaeilpour and Ahmed A. Metwally, Research Scientists, Google Research We introduce an investigational machine learning framework that translates passive wearable signals into a modifiable coachable health age, uses an action-conditioned world model to simulate personalized 12-week "what-if" habit trajectories, and expands to routine blood biomarkers to track early cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) health. Quick links Coachable health age paper CKM wearables paper Share Heart disease, kidney conditions, and metabolic disorders like type 2 diabetes aren't isolated, they form an interconnected web known as cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome . CKM progression often begins silently years before symptoms appear, shaped by everyday habits like movement, sleep, and cardiovascular activity. Catching these subtle shifts early offers the best chance to reverse the trend . Yet while smartwatches easily track what we did yesterday, moving from passive tracking to meaningful action is much harder: How do my daily habits affect my CKM right now? And if I sleep 30 minutes longer or add a brisk walk to my routine, how much will my health improve over the next three months? Age is often seen as playing a part in answering these questions, but chronological age alone isn’t enough because two people born in the same year can have vastly different physiological health. While researchers have developed “ biological clocks ” from blood tests or wearable sensors to estimate whether someone's body is aging faster or slower than their calendar age, most existing clocks aren't built for everyday coaching. Many are trained simply to estimate the birth year, latching onto traits you can't easily change, or act as black boxes that can't show how modifying a specific habit will shift your future health. In “ Personalized health coaching via coachable health age and counterfactual wearable trajectories ” and our companion study, “ Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Health Age Using Wearables and Blood Biomarkers ”, we introduce an investigational framework designed to close the loop between tracking a person’s health and actively improving it. The framework provides the following: A coachable health age model: An interpretable health-age metric built entirely from modifiable daily behaviors and physiology captured passively by consumer wearables. A sensor world model and counterfactual coaching system: A machine learning world model (SensorWM) trained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of wearable data that simulates personalized 12-week "what-if" health trajectories, paired with a language model agent that turns those simulations into realistic, clinician-vetted coaching plans. Expansion to multi-organ CKM health: When routine blood tests are available, our framework can be expanded to combine wearable streams with lab biomarkers to detect early, subclinical strain across the heart, kidney, and metabolic systems. Overview of our framework, from estimating coachable health age and predicting long-term disease risk to simulating 12-week "what-if" habit trajectories for personalized coaching. A health age metric you can actually move To make a health metric useful for coaching, every input should be something that can be tracked continuously and influenced through daily choices. Rather than training a model to guess a person’s birth year, we grounded our coachable health age (CHA) model in published epidemiological studies linking everyday behaviors to cardio-metabolic disease risk. CHA integrates four core signals passively measured by consumer wearables — resting heart rate , daily step count , sleep duration , and weekly Active Zone Minutes — alongside optional markers like VO2max, sleep schedule regularity , and insulin resistance , when available. Because active people often have lower resting heart rates and better sleep, we mathematically adjust for overlap across these signals so each habit contributes its distinct share to your health age delta , the difference between your CHA and chronological age. A negative delta (say, −3 years) means an individual's physiological profile appears younger than their chronological age, while a positive delta signals accelerated aging. We validated this model across three independent cohorts: Predicting future disease ( All of Us research program , n = 22,748): Across more than 68,000 person-years of consenting Fitbit and electronic health record follow-up, healthy participants who had a health age older than their calendar age at baseline were significantly more likely to develop hypertension, cardiovascular disease, or type 2 diabetes over the next eight years. Adding CHA to standard clinical metrics (age, sex, and BMI) significantly improved disease risk prediction, especially among adults under 50. Improvement over time (longitudinal Fitbit cohort, n = 1,464): Tracking users across consecutive 3-month windows over two years showed that among users with a sustained change in habits, the CHA decreased. Alignment with clinical health ( WEAR-ME study ): Unlike wearable aging clocks trained to predict chronological age, CHA aligned better with the modified American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 cardiovascular score and metabolic syndrome severity score , as well as participants' own self-reported health. Across 18,423 disease-free participants in the All of Us cohort, those with a health age younger than or equal to their calendar age had significantly higher disease-free survival over 8 years ( left ), while 2-year longitudinal tracking shows that individuals can meaningfully lower their health age over 3-month windows ( right ). Playing out "what-if" futures with a sensor world model Knowing your health age tells you where you stand today. Turning that number into a personalized plan requires answering a "what-if" (or counterfactual) question: What will happen to my body over the next 12 weeks if I change specific habits, and which plan can I realistically stick with? Simply plugging new step or sleep targets into a static calculator misses how the body adapts as a connected system. When you consistently move more and sleep better over several weeks, your resting heart rate and heart rate variability gradually improve too, creating extra health benefits downstream. To capture these dynamics, we developed Sensor World Model (SensorWM), an action-conditioned world model pre-trained on 2.28 million person-weeks of de-identified data from roughly 100,000 consenting Fitbit users. Given two weeks of baseline wearable data, SensorWM forecasts how 20 physiological markers will evolve over the next 12 weeks under different daily steps, sleep, and cardio routines, outperforming general-purpose time-series foundation models like TimesFM while preserving the clinical patterns associated with diabetes, hypertension, and insulin resistance. We paired SensorWM with a feasibility-constrained optimizer and a language model coaching agent to do three things: Simulate: SensorWM rolls out 125 candidate 12-week habit combinations for each person, comparing them against a "status-quo" projection if habits stay the same. Filter for realism and safety: The most aggressive workout plan doesn't help if it causes burnout in week two. Our optimizer weighs projected health-age reductions against each person's historical habit flexibility and clinical safety bounds, picking a more ambitious target (−2.3 years) for someone with high baseline flexibility, and a gentler ramp (−1.3 years) for someone whose routine is more constrained. Coach: The language model translates the top-ranked pathways into a supportive, progressive 12-week coaching plan. SensorWM simulates 12-week physiological responses under candidate habit changes and balances health-age improvement against each person's historical habit flexibility. Put to the test by lifestyle coaches and clinicians Does grounding a language model in world-model simulations actually produce better guidance than giving the exact same model a user's wearable history alone? We ran a blinded, head-to-head study with five certified lifestyle coaches and five board-certified primary care and lifestyle medicine physicians across 49 participant profiles spanning five behavioral personas (490 paired reviews total), alongside automated evaluations across the full WEAR-ME cohort ( n = 2,780). Strong expert preference: Lifestyle coaches chose the counterfactual-grounded plan as the best overall plan in 71.4% of evaluations (p < 0.001) and rated it more likely to drive long-term adherence in 71.0% of evaluations (p < 0.001). Clinician-verified safety: Physicians rated 99.2% of counterfactual plans within safe exercise intensity limits and 97.6% accurate on physiological claims. Why it worked: Both coaches and clinicians highlighted that showing people a concrete contrast between their "status-quo" trajectory and achievable "what-if" options (92% vs. 8% among clinicians) gave them a clear, motivating reason to act and a stronger sense of agency (97% vs. 59%). In blinded evaluations by certified lifestyle coaches and board-certified clinicians, counterfactual-grounded coaching plans were preferred nearly 3-to-1 over generic wearable-grounded plans while meeting 99.2% clinical safety standards. Zooming in on organ systems: Adding routine blood biomarkers for CKM health Because our health age model is modular, it can easily incorporate routine clinical lab tests when available. In our companion study , we expanded the framework to profile CKM syndrome across individual organ systems, pairing continuous wearables with occasional blood biomarkers that alone miss day to day lifestyle patterns. Conceptual framework of the multimodal CKM health age model, integrating wearable physiology with organ-specific blood biomarkers across diverse aging profiles. Early CKM decline rarely causes symptoms, and occasional clinic blood draws miss day-to-day lifestyle patterns. Evaluated in 819 WEAR-ME participants, our multimodal CKM health age model combines continuous wearable signals (resting heart rate, steps, active zone minutes, and sleep) with three routine blood biomarkers: cholesterol-to-HDL ratio (cardiovascular), eGFR (kidney filtration), and HOMA-IR (metabolic insulin resistance). By measuring how far each marker departs from healthy clinical thresholds (a normalized deviance score), the CKM model revealed that multi-organ aging doesn't follow a single template: while metabolic and cardiovascular strain are often correlated, early kidney decline frequently appears independently. Moreover, the resulting CKM health age gap aligned closely with both objective clinical scores (modified Life's Essential 8 r = −0.58; metabolic syndrome severity r = 0.65) and how healthy participants felt day to day. Population-level heterogeneity across kidney, metabolic, and cardiovascular systems (teal = healthier than reference; brown = subclinical strain), showing why personalized multi-organ profiling matters. Looking ahead Together, these studies show how consumer wearables and machine learning can help shift personal health from looking in the rearview mirror to navigating the road ahead. While our evaluations were conducted offline using retrospective research cohorts, and these models are investigational research prototypes rather than clinical diagnostic tools, they lay the foundation for future prospective trials testing how interactive "what-if" coaching can help people build lasting habits and improve their long-term health. Lee, Menglian Zhou, Marius Guerard, Sohrab Sidhu, Alexandru Solot, Hamid Palangi, Pramod Rudrapatna, Ming-Zher Poh, Max A. Xu, Daniel McDuff, Dimitrios Antos, Yuzhe Yang, Jeffrey N. Chiang (from UCLA), Anthony Z. Faranesh, Conor Heneghan, Lindsey Sunden, Mark Malhotra, Cathy Speed, Javier L. Prieto, Shwetak Patel, A. Ali Heydari, and Ahmed A. Metwally. title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
description: arXiv:2611.14320v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace

description: arXiv:2611.13843v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Typed-decision encoders answer a question about a text in one forward pass, but their behaviour outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. Labels come from Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept); an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items, and the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test text and any training text is 0.33. title: Beyond Proxy Metrics: MLLMs as Human Surrogates for Explainable AI Evaluation
description: arXiv:2611.13926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) has expanded into a broad and impactful research area, but the fundamental question of how best to evaluate explanation techniques has proven frustratingly elusive. Methodologies typically revolve around either proxy metrics which tell us little about the utility of an explanation, or human evaluation which---while generally considered the gold standard---is expensive, difficult to scale, and challenging to reproduce. In this paper, we investigate if Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can act as surrogate human participants to automate the evaluation of XAI. To do this, we first propose a ``purpose-grounded'' evaluation framework with metrics applicable to both MLLMs and human users alike. Then, we offer some conceptual insights as to why and when we can trust these models to automate this process. Lastly, we conduct extensive empirical testing across five purpose-grounded areas such as model improvement and fourteen popular MLLMs. Results indicate that all models trend positively, but OpenAI and Qwen models generally show higher alignment compared to other variants, which would be the recommended choices in practice. We expect our insights not to replace user testing, but rather to help XAI researchers complement their current evaluation methodologies and move the field away from heavy reliance on proxy metrics for measuring explanation utility.

title: TRACE: Business Rule-Grounded Reasoning Curriculum for Knowledge-Preserving Parametric Tool Retrieval in Enterprise LLMs
description: arXiv:2607.22639v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Parametric retrieval enables LLMs to retrieve tools implicitly by assigning each API a unique virtual token and training the model to generate it via constrained beam search. Toolsense shows that this regime has two critical drawbacks: it destroys parametric tool knowledge during training, and its beam-search decoding is too slow for real-time deployment. We introduce TRACE (Tool Retrieval via Augmented Chain-of-thought and Enterprise rules), a two-stage curriculum that resolves this dissociation. Stage 1 reuses the multi-format memorization SFT from ToolSense to seed tool knowledge with LoRA. Stage 2 is our core contribution: the model is trained to emit a thinking trace before producing a JSON list of tool tokens, using two data sources -- RRB pairs from ToolSense and queries synthesized to target business rules curated by domain experts -- both augmented with reasoning traces. This training objective preserves Stage 1 MCQ and QA probing accuracy while enabling single-beam greedy decoding at production latency. Evaluated on a combined enterprise catalog of 8,300+ tools across two enterprise product lines, TRACE training for Stage 2 not only preserves but improves tool understanding: MCQ accuracy gains +3.2 pp and QA probing gains +9 pp over Stage 1. On retrieval, TRACE achieves ~86% recall on Domain A and ~60% on Domain B -- compared to embedding baseline performance of ~27% & ~52% -- both with single-beam greedy decoding, making it directly deployable at production latency.

title: Activation-Guided Graph Retrieval for Cognitive Memory Reconstruction in Language Model Systems
description: arXiv:2611.13127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented language model systems generally select context by query-conditioned relevance. We argue that long-lived AI systems require a second operator: activation-conditioned memory availability. We specify an architecture in which request and goal cues seed an authorized memory graph, activation and fan attenuation allocate a bounded traversal frontier, retrieved entities recursively emit cues, and a typed evidence graph is reconstructed before generation. The specification yields five architectural consequences about candidate selection, traversal control, graph regularization, evidence reconstruction, and reinforcement. We derive implementation-level cost estimates and define ablations, failure conditions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if a simpler graph reranker matches full traversal on causal and temporal recovery under equal budgets. This architecture-and-analysis preprint reports no benchmark measurements. If the claim holds, retrieval returns the evidence path that makes a memory available, not only a ranked list.

title: From Architecture to Output: Testing the Structural Origins of Hallucination and the Amplifying Role of Data
description: arXiv:2606.07537v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Surveys of hallucination classify errors by how an output relates to its source, and often explain them by the model's structure: attention retrieves by association, the maximum-likelihood objective has no term for truth, and left-to-right decoding commits to early tokens. Data, on this account, makes these failures worse rather than causing them. The account is usually argued rather than tested. We test it with interventions that need only sampling access. Study 1 holds pretraining data, tokenizer and scale fixed and swaps attention for a state-space mixer, using five Pythia/Mamba pairs from 130M to 2.8B parameters and four further attention models, on 111 facts presented with a planted false or a planted true statement. Swapping the mixer leaves free-recall failure unchanged (both 2.8B models answer 3 of 200 SimpleQA questions), but it changes what happens to a defect in the input. From 410M upwards, every attention model repeats the planted falsehood more often than its matched state-space model (2.8B: 650 vs. 566 of 666 items, p = 2.5e-20), also on facts both models know, while the state-space models can still read planted facts they did not know. Study 2 replaces the first wrong fact in 111 erroneous answers from three instruction-tuned models. The correct fact cuts the share of answers with a downstream error from 92.5% to 48.1%, but a different wrong fact works as well (p = 0.38), and the models give the right answer in isolation on only 2 of 111 items. description: arXiv:2611.13020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electronic design automation (EDA) workflows remain highly fragmented, requiring engineers to coordinate heterogeneous representations, specialised software tools, and iterative verification across multiple design stages. title: Embodied Science Agents: Making Embodied Experimental Design Learnable
description: arXiv:2611.12958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large models have accelerated AI for Science toward agentic science, where AI agents autonomously conduct scientific discovery. Realising this vision requires closing the loop between computational reasoning and physical experimentation, positioning self-driving laboratories (SDLs) as critical enablers. However, existing SDLs exhibit a fundamental paradox: foundation model integration has increased linguistic sophistication while severing physical grounding. By treating models as disembodied planners that output symbolic workflows for separate robotic systems, current architectures inherently block the development of embodied experimental intuition. We argue that overcoming this paradox requires embedding \emph{learnability} along three interdependent axes: cognitive learnability (learning what to investigate), experimental learnability (learning where to search), and embodied learnability (learning how to act). Building on this view, we introduce the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), which unifies digital intelligence with physical embodiment through three synergistic components: a Digital Agent that provides cognitive and experimental learnability via memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent that provides embodied learnability via generalisable instrument control, and an Embodied Unified Interface for seamless coordination. We validated ESA in autonomous wastewater treatment experiments, navigating over 200 million possible conditions. Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82\% to 99.7\%, corresponding to a 98.5\% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation, while its learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, a promising step toward next-generation SDLs for autonomous scientific discovery.

description: arXiv:2605.24001v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances in one-step text-to-image generation have enabled real-time synthesis with remarkable efficiency and quality. description: arXiv:2611.12899v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural operators (NOs) have been introduced as deep learning-powered solutions to the computational bottleneck of solving families of problems. description: arXiv:2602.02711v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance in long-horizon agentic tasks through multi-step interaction and reasoning at test time. This mixed-precision design also enables nested quantization, reducing the memory footprint by 39% on average compared with FP16. Across three long-horizon agentic benchmarks with nested quantization, DMR achieves an average 2.44x decode speedup over FP16 at comparable task success rates, without fine-tuning the underlying model. title: A Comprehensive Survey of Agent Distillation across Models, Artifacts, and Harnesses
description: arXiv:2609.36630v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge distillation provides a teacher-student framework for transferring capabilities at reduced cost and has been widely studied for large language models (LLMs). This shift from model-level to agent-level knowledge transfer supports efficient deployment, broader capability access, and continual self-evolution. However, existing surveys largely examine model distillation and agent system design separately, limiting comparison of transfer strategies across agent components. To bridge this gap, we formalize Agent Distillation as persistent knowledge transfer between teacher and student agents and present its first unified survey. Distinguishing experience used for transfer from knowledge retained for reuse, we develop a knowledge-substrate taxonomy based on where knowledge persists: models, artifacts, or harnesses. Building on this taxonomy, we analyze cross-substrate transfer paths and hybrid strategies. To assess the resulting capabilities, we review benchmarks and evaluation protocols for retention, causal attribution, and deployed utility without further teacher support. This survey provides a unified basis for studying agent knowledge transfer and developing efficient, adaptable, and self-evolving agents.
